summary:
Órbita is a prototype astronaut health and environmental monitoring system developed by DataLab. It combines an ESP32-based sensing station, an OLED display, a web dashboard, and ASTRA, an interactive voice companion, with a Raspberry Pi intended as the local server.

The prototype brings environmental readings, simulated vital signs, and daily routines into an accessible interface. ASTRA recognizes user intentions through keywords and conversational context, provides predefined guidance, and supports reminders, journaling, and family communication scenarios. Configurable rules make alerts understandable and traceable.

We also explored NASA RR-1 environmental telemetry and radiation datasets to support historical-data testing.

Órbita addresses the challenge by helping crew members review indicators, understand changes, and follow routine actions when Earth-based assistance may be delayed. Its intended contribution is accessible monitoring and everyday support. It is a conceptual prototype, not a clinically validated medical device.
details:
What it does

Órbita brings astronaut monitoring and everyday support into one prototype. Its web dashboard presents crew information, vital-sign trends, environmental conditions, alerts, routines, and wellbeing records. ASTRA adds interaction through text and voice, helping users access information and follow scheduled activities.

The project considers the five human-spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile or closed environments. These hazards guide our design; the prototype does not directly measure or resolve every associated risk.

How it works

The hardware prototype uses an ESP32, an ML8511 ultraviolet sensor, an AHT temperature and humidity sensor, and an OLED display. The system architecture includes a Raspberry Pi as a local server for collecting, storing, and distributing readings.

The demonstration distinguishes physical environmental readings from simulated vital signs. The ML8511 measures ultraviolet intensity; it is not a detector of cosmic rays or a personal ionizing-radiation dosimeter.

ASTRA uses a deterministic intent-recognition engine rather than a trained language model. It normalizes text, recognizes keywords, tolerates minor spelling errors using Levenshtein distance, and maintains limited conversational context. It selects responses from a structured knowledge base and uses configurable rules to produce explanations and suggested actions.

Additional features include mission-clock reminders, completion and postponement controls, a wellbeing journal, and a simulated family-communication interface. Browser speech capabilities provide voice input and output, subject to device, browser, and service availability.

NASA resources and data

We consulted NASA Human Research Program resources to understand health risks and inform the content structure. We also analyzed NASA OSDR Environmental Data App datasets from RR-1, covering temperature, relative humidity, CO₂, and radiation.

For testing preparation, we standardized timestamps, separated flight and ground-control records, and flagged irregular intervals and prolonged constant values without deleting original measurements. Radiation units were preserved rather than automatically converted from mGy to mSv. These historical datasets provide environmental context and test inputs, not clinical validation of ASTRA.

Tools and development

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. ASTRA uses JSON knowledge and rule files, browser speech APIs, and an animated SVG orb. The software architecture separates interface components, data adapters, intent recognition, reminders, and indicator evaluation. Automated unit tests, TypeScript checks, and production builds supported development.

Benefits, creativity, and intended impact

Our contribution is the combination of physical prototyping, visual monitoring, explainable rules, and a voice companion in one interface. We aim to reduce the effort required to review information, maintain routines, and record wellbeing observations.

Design considerations included delayed communication, local operation, accessibility, individual reference values, data provenance, and clear separation between measured, simulated, and historical information. The prototype supports observation and routine follow-up; it does not diagnose conditions, prescribe treatment, or establish operational medical fitness.


AI Assistance Disclosure

We used ChatGPT, Gemini, and AI coding assistance for research, programming, debugging, test preparation, documentation, editing, translation, and data analysis. AI-assisted data processing included restructuring NASA RR-1 CSV files and transcribing a demonstration screenshot. Original NASA measurement values were preserved, and simulated vital signs were identified. ASTRA itself uses deterministic rules and predefined knowledge rather than a trained generative language model.
